stages.name: Ptolemaic
stages.desc: Held mainly by the Ptolemies of Egypt

stages.name: Seleucid
stages.desc: Held mainly by the Seleucid kings

stages.desc: Fought over, divided, or held by a third power

states.name: Cyprus
timeline: Cyprus is still held by Demetrius, son of the defeated Antigonus
Ptolemy I takes Cyprus, which becomes a lasting Ptolemaic naval base

states.name: Israel
timeline: Ptolemy I occupies the south, though the victors of Ipsus awarded Syria to Seleucus
Theodotus hands Ptolemais to Antiochus III; the Fourth Syrian War rolls south
After Raphia the towns return to Ptolemy IV
Antiochus III invades again in the Fifth Syrian War; Scopas counterattacks
The last Ptolemaic garrisons fall and the land passes to the Seleucids

states.name: Palestine
timeline: Ptolemy I holds Gaza and the hill country of Judea
Antiochus III's advance reaches the south
After Raphia, Ptolemaic rule returns
Antiochus III storms Gaza; Scopas then recovers much of the south
Antiochus III completes the conquest and is received in Jerusalem

states.name: Lebanon
timeline: Ptolemy I holds Phoenicia south of the Eleutherus, but Demetrius's garrisons keep Tyre and Sidon
Ptolemy I takes Tyre and Sidon from Demetrius: all of southern Phoenicia is Ptolemaic
In the Second Syrian War, Antiochus II takes the coast north of Sidon
The peace ending the Third Syrian War leaves Phoenicia to Egypt
Tyre goes over to Antiochus III; his army pushes down the coast
After Raphia the Phoenician cities return to Ptolemy IV
The Fifth Syrian War reaches the coast
Starved out at Sidon, Scopas surrenders and Phoenicia passes to the Seleucids

states.name: Syria
timeline: Seleucus holds the north, where he soon founds new cities; the Ptolemies hold the far south
Ptolemaic forces seize Damascus; the First Syrian War follows
Antiochus I has retaken Damascus, and peace confirms the frontier
Arwad, off this coast, becomes a free city allied to the Seleucids (see its marker)
Ptolemy III invades during the Third Syrian War
Seleucus II recovers most of Syria and relieves Damascus
From here Antiochus III first attacks Ptolemaic lands, through the Marsyas valley
Antiochus III gathers his army at Damascus and marches on Panium

states.name: Turkey
timeline: Lysimachus takes most of Anatolia; Seleucus founds Antioch in the far south within a year
Seleucus defeats Lysimachus at Corupedium and claims Anatolia, though Ptolemaic bases remain on the coast
Ptolemy III enters Antioch and takes Seleucia and the Cilician coast
Egypt keeps Seleucia; war between Seleucus II and his brother splits Seleucid Anatolia
Antiochus III retakes Seleucia, but Anatolia remains in other hands
Antiochus III captures the rebel Achaeus at Sardis and restores royal power in western Anatolia
Antiochus III moves against the remaining Ptolemaic ports of the southern coast

states.name: Jordan
timeline: The lands east of the Jordan fall under Ptolemaic rule with the rest of the south
Zenon, agent of Ptolemy's finance minister, tours the land of Ammon
Antiochus III takes Pella, Abila, Gadara and Rabbatamana
After Raphia the towns return to Ptolemy IV
After Panium, the towns east of the Jordan begin to fall to Antiochus III
The conquest of the Ptolemaic south is complete

states.name: Egypt
timeline: The heartland of the Ptolemies, ruled from Alexandria
Ptolemy IV's army, with Egyptian phalanx troops, marches out to fight at Raphia
Upper Egypt breaks away in a long revolt under a rival pharaoh
Ptolemy IV dies and a small child, Ptolemy V, inherits

states.name: N. Cyprus
timeline: Cyprus is still held by Demetrius, son of the defeated Antigonus
Ptolemy I takes Cyprus, which becomes a lasting Ptolemaic naval base

states.name: Cyprus U.N. Buffer Zone
timeline: Cyprus is still held by Demetrius, son of the defeated Antigonus
Ptolemy I takes Cyprus, which becomes a lasting Ptolemaic naval base

events.title: Battle of Ipsus
events.text: Seleucus and Lysimachus destroy Antigonus, with Seleucus's elephants cutting off the enemy cavalry, and Syria is awarded to Seleucus.

events.title: Ptolemy seizes the south
events.text: Ptolemy I occupies southern Syria and Phoenicia south of the Eleutherus, the claim behind a century of war.

events.title: Antioch founded
events.text: Seleucus founds Antioch on the Orontes, soon the heart of Seleucid Syria.

events.title: Seleucia Pieria founded
events.text: Seleucus builds the fortified port of Seleucia on the terraces above the sea.

events.title: Elephants at Apamea
events.text: Seleucus stables his Indian war elephants at Apamea on the Orontes.

events.title: Ptolemy takes Cyprus
events.text: Cyprus falls to Ptolemy I and becomes a lasting Ptolemaic naval base.

events.title: Tyre and Sidon fall
events.text: Ptolemy I takes the two great Phoenician cities from the garrisons of Demetrius.

events.title: Corupedium
events.text: Seleucus defeats Lysimachus and wins Anatolia, then is murdered within months.

events.title: Damascus seized
events.text: Ptolemaic forces take Damascus and the Marsyas valley, but Antiochus I wins the city back.

events.title: Tyre's civic era
events.text: Tyre begins counting its own years around now, a mark of civic self-government under Ptolemaic rule.

events.title: First Syrian War
events.text: Antiochus I and Ptolemy II go to war over Syria and the coasts of Anatolia.

events.title: Egypt gains Arwad
events.text: The peace, around this year, leaves Arwad and Marathos in Ptolemaic hands, making all Phoenicia Egyptian.

events.title: Elephant hunters sail
events.text: Ptolemy II puts elephant hunting on a systematic footing, shipping African animals up the Red Sea.

events.title: Enslavement decree
events.text: A royal order for Syria and Phoenicia demands the registration of livestock and of free locals seized as slaves.

events.title: Arwad goes free
events.text: Arwad begins a new civic era in autumn, a free city allied to the Seleucids, most likely by grant of Antiochus II.

events.title: A girl is sold
events.text: At Birta in Ammon, a deed records the sale of a girl named Sphragis, about seven, for fifty drachmas to Zenon.

events.title: Battle off Cos
events.text: Antigonus of Macedon's fleet defeats the Ptolemaic navy in the Aegean, around this year; the date is debated.

events.title: Berenice marries
events.text: Antiochus II sets aside Laodice and marries Ptolemy II's daughter Berenice, sealing the peace of the Second War.

events.title: Berenice murdered
events.text: After Antiochus II's death, Laodice's partisans kill Berenice and her small son at Antioch.

events.title: Ptolemy III invades
events.text: Berenice's brother enters Antioch and takes Seleucia in the Third Syrian War.

events.title: Damascus holds
events.text: Seleucus II recovers most of Syria and an Egyptian siege of Damascus fails.

events.title: Peace of 241
events.text: Egypt keeps Seleucia, the port of Antioch, along with Phoenicia and parts of Cilicia.

events.title: Failure at Gerrha
events.text: The young Antiochus III attacks through the Marsyas valley, but Theodotus holds the passes for Ptolemy.

events.title: Seleucia retaken
events.text: Antiochus III storms the port's suburb and bribes its officers, ending twenty-seven years of Ptolemaic occupation.

events.title: Theodotus changes sides
events.text: Ptolemy's governor delivers Ptolemais to Antiochus III while another officer gives up Tyre, with forty ships between them.

events.title: Battle of Porphyreon
events.text: Antiochus III forces the coastal pass north of Sidon, killing about two thousand of Nicolaus's men and capturing as many.

events.title: Arwad an ally
events.text: Polybius records Arwad joining Antiochus III as an ally rather than as a subject.

events.title: Scythopolis surrenders
events.text: Philoteria and Scythopolis give up to Antiochus III, opening Galilee and the Jordan valley.

events.title: Rabbatamana falls
events.text: Antiochus III cuts the secret water passage of the town that is now Amman, forcing its surrender.

events.title: Egyptians in the phalanx
events.text: Sosibius arms about twenty thousand native Egyptians as heavy infantry for the coming war.

events.title: Battle of Raphia
events.text: Ptolemy IV defeats Antiochus III in June, after Indian and African elephants meet in the only major battle known to match them.

events.title: Raphia decree
events.text: Egyptian priests meeting at Memphis honour Ptolemy IV for his victory.

events.title: Truce after Raphia
events.text: Antiochus III keeps Seleucia but gives up Coele-Syria and Phoenicia, and Ptolemy IV tours the cities in triumph.

events.title: Upper Egypt revolts
events.text: Horwennefer, a rival pharaoh, rules much of the south for two decades.

events.title: A child king
events.text: Ptolemy IV dies, Queen Arsinoe is murdered, and courtiers rule for the small Ptolemy V.

events.title: Fifth Syrian War
events.text: Antiochus III attacks again, while Philip V of Macedon strikes the Ptolemaic Aegean.

events.title: Gaza stormed
events.text: Antiochus III takes Gaza, the gateway to Egypt, by storm after it holds out for Ptolemy.

events.title: Scopas strikes back
events.text: Over the winter, the Aetolian general in Ptolemaic pay recovers much of Coele-Syria and Judea.

events.title: Battle of Panium
events.text: Antiochus III destroys Scopas's army by the springs of the Jordan below Mount Hermon.

events.title: Rome warns the kings
events.text: Roman envoys tell Antiochus III and Philip V not to invade Egypt itself.

events.title: Sidon surrenders
events.text: Relief armies fail, famine sets in, and Scopas gives up Sidon with his surviving men.

events.title: Jerusalem welcomes Antiochus
events.text: Antiochus III enters the city and, according to Josephus, grants it rebuilding aid and tax relief.

events.title: The coast is Seleucid
events.text: With the last Ptolemaic garrisons gone, Tyre, Sidon and the southern coast belong to Antiochus III.

chartNote: Share of the area of today's countries, by who held most of each or its main prize: a simplification, since regions are modern boundaries, not ancient ones. The real frontier ran through modern Syria and Turkey, so their colour hides Ptolemaic Seleucia and Cilicia and the fight for Damascus. Egypt and Turkey dominate the shares. Arwad, a free city from 259 BC, is too small to fill and appears only as a marker. Dates are often debated.
